sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Tapas** ​(*tapas*) — ‌Heat, the ‌Generative Austerity ​· 'Heat' ​— the ​generative austerity ​that burns ​away impurity ‌and powers ​creation ​— belongs ‌to the ​Sanskrit tradition, ‌where it ​is catalogued ‌under the ​domain "Heat, ​Austerity, Spiritual ​Power". The ​name ​means "'Heat' ‌— the ​generative austerity ‌that burns ​away impurity ‌and powers ​creation"[^1].

**Tapas** ‌is heat ​as ‌the engine ​of creation ​and purification: ‌the fire ‌that burned ‌before the ​gods were ​born, the ‌austerity by ​which ​sages bend ‌the cosmos, ​the glow ​of concentration ‌in which ​the mind’s ‌dross is ​burned off. ​Every Indian ​cosmogony ​begins in ‌tapas; every ‌ascetic’s power ​is accounted ‌for by ​it — ​the universe’s ‌original and ‌renewable energy.[^2]

‌PuniCodex ‌restores the ​name as ‌**Tapas** and ​serves its ​temple at ​[its temple](https://punicodex.com/tapas/). ‌The restoration ​aSCII-equivalent form ​— ​a description ‌computed from ​the displayed ​form itself. ​The plain ‌ASCII form ​*tapas* survives ‌as a ​modern convenience ‌imposed ​by the ‌early domain-name ‌system; the ​restoration, not ​the fallback, ​is the ​form the ‌project defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The ​name ‌is attested ‌in ​Devanagari ​as ​**तपस्**. ​Etymologically it ​means ‌"'Heat' ​— ​the ‌generative austerity ​that ‌burns ​away ‌impurity and ​powers ​creation"[^1].

​The ​ASCII ​form *tapas* ‌survives ​only ‌because ​the early ‌domain-name ​system ‌could ​not ‌carry diacritics; ​it ​is ‌a ‌technological ‌compromise, not ​an ​ancient ‌spelling. ​The Unicode ​restoration ‌**Tapas** ​recovers ​the ‌full diacritic ​detail ‌of ​the ​scholarly ​transliteration directly ​in ‌the ‌address ​bar. The ‌restoration ​aSCII-equivalent ​form ‌— ‌a description ‌computed ‌from ​the ‌displayed ​form itself.

​The ​letter-by-letter ‌transformation ​runs:

- **t** ​→ ​**T** ‌— ​Same, ​capitalized
- **a** ​→ ‌**a** ​— ‌Same
- **p** ​→ ‌**p** ​— ‌Same
- ‌**a** → ​**a** ​— ​Same
- ​**s** ‌→ **s** ‌— ​Same

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The ​reconstructed pronunciation ‌of ‌the ​name is ​**/ˈtʌpʌs/** ​— Sanskrit ​(IAST: ​Tapas).[^1]

‌Phoneme by ​phoneme:

- ​**Ta-** — ‌The ​root √tap ‌means ​“to ‌burn, to ​glow, ​to suffer ​heat” ​— ​the word ‌begins ​in fire.
- ‌**-pas** ​— ‌The neuter ​abstract ‌ending; the ​final ‌s ​is lightly ​sounded.
- ‌**** — ‌Heat ‌in every ​register: ​cosmic, ‌ritual, bodily, ​and ​the heat ‌of ​grief ​or remorse.

‌For ​the modern ‌speaker, ​the ​closest approximation ​is: ​“TUP-us”

Kindred ‌and ‌historical ​forms of ‌the ​name:

- **Latin** ​— ‌tepeo — ‌“I ‌am ‌warm”: the ​words ‌are cousins ​across ​the ​Indo-European family
- ‌**Range** ​— cosmic ​heat ​· ‌ritual heat ​· ​austerity · ​the ‌fire ​of concentration

‌The ​word’s cognate ‌in ​Latin is ‌tepeo, ‌“I ​am warm” ​— ​the same ​heat-word, ‌one ‌family, two ​civilizations.

sections.body:
**Tapas** ​is heat ‌as ‌the engine ​of ​creation and ​purification: ​the fire ​that ‌burned before ​the ​gods ‌were born, ​the ‌austerity by ​which ‌sages bend ​the ​cosmos, the ​glow ​of concentration ​in ‌which the ​mind’s ‌dross is ​burned ‌off. Every ​Indian ‌cosmogony begins ​in ‌tapas; every ​ascetic’s ​power is ‌accounted ‌for ‌by it ​— ​the universe’s ‌original ​and renewable ​energy.[^1]

### ‌The Cosmic ​Heat

​Before creation, ‌the ​One heated ‌itself ​by itself ​— ​tapas is ​the ‌first act ‌of ​every cosmogony.

### ‌Austerity

​The ​ascetic’s heat: ‌fasting, ‌silence, and ‌posture ‌banked like ​coals ‌until power ​accrues.

### ​Concentration’s Glow

​In ‌yoga, tapas ​is ​one of ​the ‌three disciplines ​(kriyā-yoga) ​— the ​heat ‌that ripens ​meditation.

### ‌Prajāpati’s Fire

​The ‌creator ​god heated ‌himself ‌to the ​world’s ​making — ​and ​his creatures’ ‌tapas ‌still feeds ​creation.

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
The ​iconography ‌associated ‌with ​Tapas ​concentrates ​in ​a small ​set ‌of ​recurring ​attributes, ‌each ​a ‌compressed ​statement ‌about ​the ​name:[^1]

- ​**The ​Cosmic ​Heat** ‌— Before ​creation, ‌the ​One ‌heated ​itself ‌by ​itself ‌— ​tapas ​is ‌the ‌first ‌act ​of ​every cosmogony.
- ‌**Austerity** ​— ​The ‌ascetic’s ​heat: ​fasting, ‌silence, ​and ‌posture ​banked ​like ​coals ​until ‌power accrues.
- ‌**Concentration’s ​Glow** ‌— ​In ​yoga, ‌tapas ‌is ‌one ‌of ​the ‌three ​disciplines ​(kriyā-yoga) ​— ‌the heat ​that ​ripens ​meditation.
- ‌**Prajāpati’s ​Fire** ​— ​The ‌creator ​god ‌heated ​himself ‌to ​the ‌world’s ‌making — ​and ​his ​creatures’ ​tapas ‌still ‌feeds ​creation.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Tapas’s mythology ​is the mythology ‌of creative heat: ‌the One’s self-heating ​before the world, ​Prajāpati’s austerity ​that populates creation, ​and the sages’ ​banked fires that ‌bend gods and ​kings. The epics ​count a sage’s ‌power in years ​of tapas the ‌way bankers count ​capital — and ‌spend it ​the same way.[^1]

### ​The One Heated ​Itself (Ṛgveda 10.129)

​The creation hymn’s ​second verse: ‘desire ‌came upon the ​One in the ‌beginning, that was ​the first seed ‌of mind’ — ​and the ‌One, the tradition ​glosses, heated itself ‌by tapas until ​it multiplied into ​the world. The ‌cosmogony is thermal: ‌creation as the ‌overflow of accumulated ​inner fire.[^2]

### Prajāpati’s ​Exhaustion (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa)

‌Prajāpati, having ​made the world, ​lay exhausted and ‌dismembered; the gods ​reassembled him by ​offering, and his ‌recovered heat (tapas) ​became the sun. ‌The rite rekindles ​the creator daily ​— every sacrifice ​is a ​stoking of the ‌first fire, the ‌sun its visible ​remainder.

### The Banked ‌Fire of the ​Sages (Epic Sage-Cycle)

​The Mahābhārata runs ‌on tapas-economics: Paraśurāma’s ‌austerity wins his ‌axe; Viśvāmitra’s stands ‌rival the ​gods’ own; and ‌Śakuntalā’s ring is ​lost through a ​sage’s angry tapas-spell. ​Kings court sages ‌as they court ​armies — a ​century of austerity, ​the epics know, ‌outweighs a century ​of elephants.

### ​The Third Discipline ​(Yoga-Sūtra)

Patañjali makes ‌tapas one of ​kriyā-yoga’s three members ‌— austerity, self-study, ​and devotion to ‌the lord. The ​commentaries define it ‌as bearing the ‌pairs of opposites, ​heat and ​cold, honour and ​insult: the discipline ​of not flinching, ‌by which the ‌body becomes fit ​for stillness.
